heading: Abstract
note: One 332-word display abstract: the objectives, minimised crossovers with maximum campsite use and a matched trip-length mix, and the three models named in turn, the Priority Model, the density perturbation algorithm and the bone growth model. Stored count 2 counts the title lines above it; blocks 1-3, the title, the team number and the date, are front matter.

heading: 1 Introduction (with the model overview)
note: The chapter opens with a running head glued to the 1 Introduction heading and then the problem setting, the mile 0 to mile 225 river, the 7 to 19 day trips with 6 to 18 nights, and the evenly spaced campsites (5-6). The difficulty is then stated, that variety, non-passing and non-crossing are hard together and that queueing and scheduling theory do not transfer (7-8), and the four attempts are summarised in turn, naive (9), priority (10), density perturbation (11) and bone growth with its 2 Definitions and Variables heading glued on (12). Stored count 7 agrees.

heading: 2 Definitions and Variables
note: The definition list, one job per printed bullet: the lead-in (13), crossover (14), trip with its page split (15-16), X (17), Y (18), T (19), P (20), the two schedule matrix formats S1 and S2 with their line-split explanations (21-24), the open campsite percentage as fractions of unoccupied campsites over the 180 days (25-27), Dmax (28-29), the problem statement as one bullet (30-33), and the carrying capacity C(Y) = max X(Y)/Y with the 3 Assumptions heading glued on (34-36). heading: 3 Assumptions (3.1 to 3.6)
note: Six numbered assumptions. 3.1 assumes only trip length matters and quotes the 2007 to 2010 Colorado River vessel counts of about 415 motor against 183 non-motor (37-38), then argues oar and motor trips can be scheduled independently (39). 3.2 forbids switching boats mid-trip (40). 3.3 fixes the guaranteed motor distance at 64 miles a day from 8 mph over 8 hours (41). 3.4 uses the Colorado and Salmon campsite counts, 162 over 250 miles and 185 over 180.6 miles, and Figure 1's spacing histogram (42-44), then tests spacings of 5, 1.5 and 1 mile a campsite, Y = 45, 150 and 225 (45). 3.5 removes equipment and labour limits (46-47) and 3.6 ignores daytime congestion, penalising crossovers instead (48-49). Stored count 10 agrees.

heading: 4 Models (opening)
note: The section opener: optimal is defined as a schedule with no two trips on the same campsite on the same night (50), and the problem is placed against scheduling and queueing theory, n activities each needing Y+1 precedence-ordered jobs on river sections as machines, which balking queues do not cover (51). Stored count 3 against two printed units; the third stored paragraph is the 4.1 heading, coded with its own chapter.

heading: 4.1 Naive model
note: The first algorithm: an empty schedule filled one trip at a time (52), three bullets of the general idea, random trip, insert if it fits anywhere, else drop the length from the distribution (53-55), the input and while loop with step 1 (56-57), step 2's tolerance search over nights with the four substeps, equal river portions, nearest free campsite, tolerance failure, success when every night is covered (58-63), the break on success (64), Figure 2's three-trip walk-through (65), the failure branch (66), the two stated problems, no regard for crossovers and long trips blocking short ones (67-69), and the decision to drop the model from formal testing with the 4.2 Priority Model heading glued on (70). Stored count 14 against ten printed units.

heading: 4.2 Priority Model and 4.3 Density Perturbation Algorithm
note: 4.2 fills the schedule one night at a time, prioritising the highest ratio of distance remaining to days remaining: four bullets of the idea, priority, cooperation between trips, crossover avoidance and removal of unschedulable trips (71-74), Figure 3 and the day loop with the probability p of sorting against a random shuffle (75-78), the per-trip campsite choice, the conflict branch with its range, removal, ranking by crossover then proximity, and the close (79-88). 4.3 then drops the assumption that any trip matters more than another and lets crossovers run free (89), moves every boat to its equal-distance position in continuous miles, with equation 1's signed density kernel and equation 2's summed density vector (90-91), iterates until boats are nearly a campsite apart (92), favours matching preferences over a fixed season schedule (93), reports 1978 trips in 180 days over 200 campsites in Figure 4 (94), and closes with the mile 10 to 215 campsite layout and the 4.4 heading (95). Stored count 22 against 15 printed units.

heading: 4.4 Bone Growth Model
note: The model that guarantees no crossovers: the motivation, symmetry and a deterministic algorithm that beats the previous attempts at launch-time uniformity (96), the two-heuristic plan (97). Heuristic 1, long trips set the rate, requires the shortest launch to outlast the longest trip still on the river (98-100), so launches alternate 6 up to 18 and back down (101). Heuristic 2 packs to the centre, defining feasibility as squeezing every trip to the centre trajectory (102-103). Then Figure 5's four panels (104) and the outline, bone sequence and target distribution (105), the add-a-trip step (106), insertion points from Heuristic 1 (107), build from the centre (108), spread out in time (109-110), try the next best trip on failure (111), repeat with a new bone (112), the greedy score criterion (113), the Figure 5 walk-through over 43 days (114), Figure 6's motor against oar colouring (115), and the oar extension left unfinished with the 5 Testing and Results heading glued on (116). Stored count 13 against 18 printed units.

heading: 5 Testing and Results (5.1 to 5.3)
note: The three-level criterion, trips and campsites first, then crossovers, then distribution match, with the no-shared-campsite condition checked on every schedule (117). 5.1 compares the Bone Growth and Priority models at Y = 45, 150 and 225 under uniform and triangle targets with the weight 40 minus length (118). 5.2 gives carrying capacities of 12.13, 12.66 and 12.94 trips a campsite for uniform and 12.33, 13.45 and 13.05 for triangle as campsites rise, while crossovers grow exponentially (119-120), with Figure 7 for Y = 225 uniform (121). 5.3 fixes the two bone structures, the alternating 6 and 18 and the descending 6 with 18 down to 10 (122), reports that both saturate out the long trips and that Bones1 tracks uniform while Bones2 does not track triangle (123), and shows Figure 8 (124). Stored count 15 against eight printed units; the stored layout counts table cells and figure panels.

heading: 6 Analysis of Results
note: The cross-model audit: five measures, trips per season, length distribution, open campsite share, crossovers per trip and carrying capacity (125-129), carrying capacity read as trips over campsites or equivalently from the filled share (130), the shared bias toward short trips (131), the opposite trends with more campsites, Priority improving on distribution while Bone Growth skews, and Priority crossovers climbing to about 29 a trip (132), and the removal experiment, dropping the most-crossing trips cost 10 to 15 percent campsite coverage while Bone Growth stayed consistent (133). Stored count 9 against six printed units.

heading: Strengths and Weaknesses (Priority Model, then Bone Growth Model)
note: Two bullet lists under their own headings. Priority strengths, high carrying capacity with a high campsite share and trip count, and low daily distance variance (134-135). Priority weaknesses, no crossover resolution with a second-pass suggestion (136-139), no reuse of freed space right after a removal (140-141), distribution distortion since long trips keep low distance-left ratios and face more removals (142-145), sensitivity to the daily departure count, whose working range is 12 to 20 (146-149), sensitivity to the input distribution, which had to be skewed long to come out uniform (150-152), and sensitivity to the sort probability, useful at 0.3 to 0.6 (153-155). Bone Growth strengths, no crossovers at all, even spread along the river and across the 180 days, and scalability to oar rafts (156-159). Bone Growth weaknesses, the trip and coverage cost of forbidding crossovers (160), sensitivity to the bone structure with the better hand-built sequences noted (161-164), trips pushed to their speed limit (165-166), and bursty launch and arrival days with the 7 Conclusion heading glued on (167). Stored count 18 against 13 printed units.

heading: 7 Conclusion
note: Two units: the summary that the naive and density models underperformed while Priority and Bone Growth covered about 80 and 50 percent of campsites, with the advice to managers on which to choose (168), and the outlook, distribution-shaped launches, varied speeds along the river, and the hypothesis that more work on Bone Growth or density perturbation could reach a global optimum, with the Memo heading glued on (169). Stored count 4 against two printed units.

heading: Memo
note: The letter to the Big Long River managers: the header (170), the two working algorithms with 70 to 50 percent campsite coverage and a carrying capacity of about 12.5 to 7.5 trips a campsite over 180 days (171), the deliverables, a per-night site list plus a master trip list, with launch times spread over the season (172), the caveats about First Launch and Final Exit capacity and uniform speed (173), and the choice between the two models, Priority for coverage with crossovers and Bone Growth for no crossovers at two-thirds the coverage, with the mix suggestion and the sign-off, the References heading glued on (174). Stored count 5 agrees.
